extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal education funding (K-12 and higher education), Title IX coordinators, institutional legal counsel, and school administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble guidance to the final Title IX regulations (§106.11 and related provisions) describing when Title IX applies, the scope of recipients' obligations (including off-campus and foreign conduct), interactions with other laws (FERPA/GEPA, constitutional due process), and related procedural expectations for institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraterritorial application of Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX (20 U.S.C. 1681) does not have extraterritorial application based on the statute's plain text and the judicial presumption against extraterritoriality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Title IX's text limits protection to 'No person in the United States,' the Department declines to treat §106.11 as extending Title IX to conduct occurring outside the United States (e.g., study abroad). The presumption against extraterritoriality (EEOC v. Aramco; Morrison; Kiobel) means statutes are interpreted as domestic unless Congress clearly indicates otherwise. As a result, recipients are not obligated under Title IX to address sex discrimination occurring outside the U.S.; however, they may independently respond under their own codes of conduct. Concerns about conflicts with foreign privacy laws (e.g., GDPR) are addressed by noting Title IX does not preempt such laws when conduct occurred abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to address hostile environment in U.S. even when some conduct occurred abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient has a responsibility to address a sex-based hostile environment in its education program or activity in the United States, even when some conduct alleged to be contributing to that hostile environment occurred outside the recipient's program or outside the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a recipient must address alleged conduct that occurred abroad depends on the particular facts and circumstances (e.g., a student assaulted abroad by a professor who then returns to campus may create a hostile on-campus environment). The Department clarifies that §106.11 requires addressing the hostile environment that exists under the recipient's U.S. education program or activity. Investigative approaches and remedies will be fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may address out-of-country conduct via institutional policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the regulations prohibits a recipient from responding to incidents that occur abroad under its existing code of conduct or other institutional policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Title IX does not impose an obligation for extraterritorial application, institutions retain discretion to investigate or discipline under their own policies for off‑campus or foreign conduct; doing so is not precluded by the Title IX regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of conduct in buildings owned/controlled by officially recognized student organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that occurs in buildings owned or controlled by a student organization officially recognized by a recipient may be considered part of the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official recognition is an institutional determination and may be present when the institution exerts oversight over the organization or can discipline it. Title IX's statutory exemptions (e.g., membership practices of social fraternities and sororities at 20 U.S.C. 1681(a)(6) and single-sex living facilities at 20 U.S.C. 1686) remain, but exemptions do not blanket-exempt such organizations from all other forms of sex discrimination (e.g., sex-based harassment of participants in programs offered by such organizations). §106.11 applies to all recipients (including elementary and secondary schools) and does not mean application is limited to postsecondary institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of §106.11 to all recipients (including K-12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.11 applies to all recipients of Federal financial assistance covered by Title IX, not solely postsecondary institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The use of 'postsecondary institution' in examples does not limit the regulation; the provision applies to elementary, secondary, and postsecondary recipients alike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct subject to a recipient's disciplinary authority determines Title IX scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct occurring off campus is included within a recipient's education program or activity when such conduct is 'subject to a recipient's disciplinary authority.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department retains the phrase 'subject to a recipient's disciplinary authority' as reflecting the administrative/scope inquiry (consistent with Davis and subsequent case law). Federal courts have found that disciplinary authority and substantial control over the context are key factors (e.g., Brown; Marshall Univ.; Pogorzelska). The regulation does not require institutions to police all student life; rather, when a recipient has knowledge of conduct that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination and that conduct is subject to disciplinary authority, the Title IX Coordinator must take prompt and effective action (§106.44(a), (f)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: No affirmative monitoring duty; obligation triggered by knowledge/report
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are not required to affirmatively monitor all student life or online activity, but when an employee or the institution has information that reasonably may indicate a sex-based hostile environment, notification and response obligations attach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department confirms recipients are not expected to proactively monitor students' online activity. However, if an employee or another party has information about conduct (including social media) that reasonably may have created a hostile environment, employees must comply with notification requirements (§106.44(c)) and the recipient must respond promptly and effectively under §106.44(a)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-specific 'similar context' and 'reasonable ability' limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations about whether conduct is within disciplinary authority, what constitutes a 'similar context,' and the scope of investigative obligations are fact-specific and depend on each recipient's circumstances and reasonable ability to investigate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a recipient already addresses certain off-campus misconduct (e.g., nonsexual assault or theft) in similar contexts, it may not disclaim responsibility for addressing sex discrimination in analogous circumstances. Nonetheless, the obligation to investigate off-campus conduct is limited by the recipient's reasonable ability to do so; institutions must assess scope on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits and burdens of §106.11 (streamlining vs resource concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.11 is intended to provide clarity and reduce confusing two-track systems by making clear when conduct is within a recipient's education program or activity, but commenters raised concerns about potential added caseloads and administrative costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department acknowledges possible increased caseloads but, based on prior experience and the Regulatory Impact Analysis, does not anticipate a meaningful increase in burdens for many recipients and believes the public‑interest benefits of uniformly addressing sex discrimination justify any added costs. Many recipients historically used alternative proceedings to address off-campus misconduct; §106.11 may change procedural paths but not necessarily the underlying duties institutions already exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile environment standard balanced with First Amendment protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of 'sex-based harassment' is tailored so that a finding of a sex-based hostile environment must be based on the totality of the circumstances, be both subjectively and objectively offensive, and be so severe or pervasive that it limits or denies participation in or the benefits of the education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation protects constitutional rights by excluding isolated comments from typically meeting the hostile-environment threshold. Title IX does not regulate speech content per se; §106.6(d) reiterates that nothing in the regulations requires a recipient to restrict First Amendment rights. Where protected speech affects the community, recipients may take responsive non-disciplinary actions (supportive measures, education) and must ensure response actions themselves comport with constitutional protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of religious exemptions and ministerial-exception concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX's statutory religious exemption applies to education programs/activities operated by entities controlled by religious organizations; it does not automatically extend to student religious organizations not controlled by a religious organization or to individual students/employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters asked for expansion of religious exemptions or carve-outs for student religious groups; the Department declined. The Department notes uncertainty in the law about applying the ministerial exception to Title IX (Supreme Court has not ruled definitively), but reiterates §106.6(d) instructing recipients not to take actions that would violate First Amendment protections. Where courts later find ministerial-exception applicability, recipients must comply with constitutional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction of Title IX with FERPA/GEPA and constitutional due process (overrides)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must comply with both Title IX and FERPA unless a direct conflict exists; statute (GEPA/20 U.S.C. 1221(d)) and regulation text incorporate a GEPA override that Title IX obligations are not obviated by FERPA. Additionally, Title IX/regulations will not be administered in a manner that requires denial of constitutionally protected due process rights (constitutional override).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departments maintain that institutions should interpret Title IX and FERPA to avoid conflict. Where direct conflicts arise (fact-specific), Title IX's requirements override conflicting FERPA provisions pursuant to GEPA; likewise, where necessary to protect constitutional due process (notice and meaningful opportunity to respond per Mathews v. Eldridge), the constitutional override may supersede FERPA. The final regulations (e.g., §§106.45(c),(f),(g) and 106.46(c),(e),(f)) include procedural protections to safeguard due process rights and inform how evidence access and other issues interact with FERPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarification and precise regulatory wording (§106.11 phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory text was revised to replace 'even if sex-based harassment' with 'even when some conduct alleged to be' in final §106.11 to clarify obligations regarding hostile environments involving some out-of-program or out-of-U.S. conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change clarifies that the recipient must address a sex-based hostile environment in its education program or activity in the United States even when some of the alleged contributing conduct occurred outside the recipient's program or outside the United States; it focuses obligations on the existence of the hostile environment in the recipient's program rather than on the location of each discrete act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee notification and evidence-access obligations in cross-jurisdictional contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: When investigating hostile environments that may involve conduct outside the U.S. or outside the recipient's program, employees and recipients remain subject to notification requirements and must consider applicable foreign privacy laws when seeking information abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department reiterates employees' duties under §106.44(c) to report information, and notes that because Title IX lacks extraterritorial effect, recipients are not independently required to respond to incidents abroad; however, if a recipient, in addressing a U.S.-based hostile environment, seeks evidence or information from another country, nothing in the regulations preempts applicable foreign privacy laws (e.g., GDPR).
